content:
As Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. heads out this fall to campaign for Republicans ahead of the midterm elections, the mode of transportation he has chosen is drawing outside scrutiny.

A Washington Post report published late Thursday found that Kennedy was given approval to use military private aircraft while traveling across the United States. Two officials told the paper that one such instance occurred on Aug. 17, when Kennedy boarded a U.S. Air Force-operated Gulfstream private jet from Washington, D.C., to Des Moines, Iowa, for an event co-hosted with Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks.

The Department of Defense charged approximately $9,000 per hour for the Gulfstream aircraft, compared to about $250 for a commercial flight covering the same distance by a federal employee.

Five individuals told The Washington Post that lawyers at the White House and the Department of Health and Human Services had signed off on the flight arrangements.

Officials described Kennedy's use of military aircraft as "rare" and emphasized that the secretary has flown commercially on multiple trips. However, the report noted that the controversy over Kennedy's travel reflects how Trump in his second term has "taken a more relaxed approach to travel arrangements for some of his Cabinet members."

During Trump's first term, former Health and Human Services Secretary Tom Price resigned amid controversy over his use of private planes. Former Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin and former Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke also became entangled in similar controversies, prompting the White House to establish new restrictions on Cabinet officials' use of private aircraft.

Kennedy has meanwhile joined a recent string of sitting Trump administration officials whose travel arrangements have come under fire.

House Judiciary Committee member Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., and Senate Judiciary Committee ranking member Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., announced in July that they were investigating FBI Director Kash Patel over allegations that he had used public resources for private jet travel and other travel perks.

The same month, the head of the Secret Service unit tasked with protecting Vice President JD Vance told MS NOW that several of Vance's requests—including the use of government helicopters to ferry him and one of his young sons to a golf lesson—were "inappropriate and without precedent."

Vance's office responded to the outlet's reporting with a statement that read, in part: "Protecting a vice president who carries significant policy responsibilities and has a young and growing family does present unique challenges, but Secret Service personnel carry out their duties with excellence every day."
